selected.title: Who calls the leak
selected.texas_link: Percepto Corporation is based in Austin, and Chevron described piloting its drone in the Permian Basin of West Texas. The film draws generic oil and gas equipment in the Permian as an illustration and names no real site.

movement.action: approved an Austin company's autonomous infrared drone as an alternative method for periodic methane leak screening
movement.object: Percepto Air Max optical gas imaging drone system

selected.why_today: On October 7th, 2026 EPA said it will propose to rescind its separate satellite and aircraft Super Emitter Program, which is already delayed to January 22nd, 2027, so the operator's own drone screening is the route in the record that stays in place.
selected.consequence: An operator's drone footage flags emissions only after a certified inspector reviews it, and that review triggers a follow-up inspection of the equipment.
selected.application_change: Methane screening at oil and gas sites can move from a person walking with a camera to a drone that flies a preset route from a station beside the equipment, with a certified person still reviewing the footage.
selected.counter_image: No source shows what the artificial intelligence does in the review, how many leaks any Permian drone has found, or any repair. The EPA letter mentions AI only in a protocol title.
selected.earned_take: Under this approval a certified person calls the leak, and what the software adds isn't in the record.

agency.next_step: EPA said on October 7th, 2026 that its proposal to rescind the Super Emitter Program is coming in days, and the program is otherwise delayed to January 22nd, 2027.
agency.who_can_act: Operators choose whether to use the approved method, EPA writes the rules, and the public can comment once the proposal is published.

filmability.viewer_question: When a drone flags a leak over oil and gas equipment, who decides it is one?
filmability.opening_action: An illustrated drone lifts from a weatherproof station beside oil and gas equipment in the Permian and flies a preset route, disclosed as Illustration.
filmability.mechanism: Input: infrared video of each point of interest on a preset flight plan. Transformation: a certified optical gas imaging inspector reviews the footage and identifies any emissions. Result: that review triggers a follow-up inspection. Limit: the letter doesn't say what the artificial intelligence does in the review.
filmability.human_consequence: Operators and the certified inspectors who review the footage and the crews who answer a follow-up inspection. No person is named and no leak count, repair or outcome is claimed.
filmability.source_limit: The EPA letter approves a method and mentions AI only in a protocol title. The AI alert claim is the companies' own, carried by trade press. No Permian result, site, county or leak count is published, and the Chevron pilot was slated to end in 2025.
three_key_images: An illustrated drone leaving its weatherproof station and flying a route over oil and gas equipment
An illustrated infrared view of a valve with a bookmark on the footage, then a certified inspector's review of that footage
A record card reading AI appears only in a protocol title beside a satellite program tag reading delayed to January 22nd, 2027

action_support.relationship: EPA's letter says a certified OGI inspector reviews the survey footage to identify any emissions.

action_support.pictured_action: A follow-up inspection tag moves to the flagged valve, then a record card reads AI appears only in a protocol title.
action_support.scope_fit: Disclosed illustration of the letter's follow-up sentence and the absence finding. It shows no repair and no outcome.
action_support.relationship: EPA's letter says the review triggers a follow-up inspection and names AI only in a protocol title.

visual_stakes.affected_group: Operators and the certified inspectors who review drone footage at oil and gas sites.
visual_stakes.physical_subject: a drone in a weatherproof station beside a valve and its infrared footage
visual_stakes.visible_change: the drone flies its route, a bookmark marks the footage, a certified inspector marks the emission, and a follow-up inspection tag lands on the valve
visual_stakes.consequence: a certified person, not the software, identifies the emission and triggers the follow-up
visual_stakes.opening_question: When a drone flags a leak over oil and gas equipment, who decides it is one?
visual_stakes.answer: Under EPA's approval a certified inspector reviews the footage and identifies any emissions, and the software's role is not in the record.
visual_stakes.asset_fit: Authored illustration only. No photographs are admitted, so no rights are in question.
visual_stakes.affected_person: No person is drawn. The inspector appears only as a review panel and a certificate mark, disclosed as illustration.
